title: Leveraging Small LLMs for Argument Mining in Education: Argument Component Identification, Classification, and Assessment
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether small, open-source large language models can be used for educational argument mining on student essays. The core problem is how to automatically segment argumentative essays into components, classify those components by rhetorical type, and assess their quality in ways that could eventually support targeted feedback for student writing. The authors position this as an accessibility, privacy, and efficiency problem in education: high-performing models often require substantial computational resources, whereas smaller open-source models could potentially run locally on students’ computers.

The study evaluates three small LLMs—Qwen 2.5 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemma 2 9B—using two adaptation approaches: few-shot prompting and fine-tuning. These models are applied to three tasks on argumentative essays: segmentation into argument components, classification into seven Toulmin-inspired categories, and quality assessment into three levels. Performance is compared against encoder-based baselines from prior work (Longformer and BERT variants) and against GPT-4o mini as a commercial benchmark. The work is framed as an empirical model-comparison study rather than a classroom intervention trial.

The population consists of essays written by U.S. students in grades 6–12 from the Feedback Prize / PERSUADE 2.0-related dataset. The subset used includes about 6,900 essays overall, with the reported train/validation/test splits drawn from prior work. The educational context is secondary student argumentative writing in English, but the models are evaluated offline on an existing benchmark dataset rather than being deployed with teachers or students in live instruction.

The main conclusions are that small open-source LLMs outperform the reported encoder baselines for argument segmentation and argument-type classification, especially when fine-tuned. Fine-tuning was particularly helpful for segmentation and type classification, while few-shot prompting worked better than fine-tuning for quality assessment. The authors argue that these results show promise for privacy-preserving, locally run writing-support tools, but they also note important limitations: poor performance on quality assessment, inference instability in some setups, and uncertain generalizability beyond English essays from U.S. grade 6–12 students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/model-comparison study on an annotated corpus of student essays, not a K-12 intervention trial with learners receiving treatment versus comparison instruction. It has clear methods and quantitative results, but no causal design or direct student outcome evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising task-performance gains for automated writing feedback components, but impact on actual student writing outcomes is indirect and unclear. Reported gains are model-performance improvements rather than student learning effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Small open-source LLMs and GPT-4o mini are used to automatically segment student essays into argument components, classify argument types, and assess argument quality as a pipeline for potential real-time writing feedback on argumentative essays.
LLM-based analysis of student argumentative writing to support improvement of essay structure and argumentation quality, positioned as a writing-support tool rather than a full tutor.

finding.finding_summary: On benchmark argumentative essay processing tasks using essays from grade 6–12 students, fine-tuned small LLMs outperformed encoder baselines for segmentation and argument-type classification. The best small open model (fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B) reached segmentation macro-F1=87.52, improving 18.05 points over Longformer; for type classification with inferred segmentation it achieved macro-F1=51.45, 12.27 points above the Longformer+BERT baseline. For quality assessment, results were weaker: the best small open model under inferred segmentation (Gemma 2 9B, 3-shot) was only roughly comparable to baseline, indicating gains are task-dependent.
finding.measure: Macro-averaged F1 for argument segmentation, argument type classification, and argument quality assessment on student argumentative essays
finding.study_size: test set: 419 essays, 3,711 arguments; training set: 3,353 essays, 29,440 arguments; validation set: 419 essays, 3,614 arguments
finding.effect_size: segmentation +18.05 F1 points vs baseline; type classification +12.27 F1 points vs baseline; quality assessment improvement not clearly established under inferred segmentation
finding.std_deviation: reported as error bars across 3 runs, exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that small open-source LLM pipelines can run locally and efficiently enough for educational deployment, including fine-tuning on a single A100 GPU and inference on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with 32GB RAM via Ollama. However, this is demonstrated as computational feasibility and accessibility rather than with direct classroom productivity or teacher-workload outcome data.
finding.measure: Technical feasibility/accessibility indicators such as local inference capability, model size, and computational setup

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that automated argument mining feedback could support students' argumentation and critical analysis of essays by identifying strengths and weaknesses in claims, evidence, counterclaims, and rebuttals. Empirically, the study measures model performance on argument-structure identification rather than direct student gains in critical thinking, so evidence for durable-skill improvement is indirect.
finding.measure: Automated identification/classification of argumentative components and their quality in student essays
